## Data load and preparation before modelling

The data are the 2016 General Social Survey extract supplied in the
[homework template](https://github.com/uoeIDS/hw-03-template). The following
preparation follows the assignment: missing values are removed before any
responses are recoded.

```{r read_data}
gss16 <- read.csv("data/gss16.csv")
```

#### Cleaning and selecting columns

```{r select-complete-cases}
gss16_advfront <- gss16 %>%
  select(advfront, emailhr, educ, polviews, wrkstat) %>%
  drop_na()
```

#### Re-levelling `advfront`

```{r recode-advfront}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = case_when(
      advfront == "Strongly agree" ~ "Agree",
      advfront == "Agree" ~ "Agree",
      TRUE ~ "Not agree"
    ),
    advfront = fct_relevel(advfront, "Not agree", "Agree")
  )
```

#### Re-levelling `polviews`

```{r recode-polviews}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    polviews = case_when(
      str_detect(polviews, "[Cc]onservative") ~ "Conservative",
      str_detect(polviews, "[Ll]iberal") ~ "Liberal",
      TRUE ~ polviews
    ),
    polviews = fct_relevel(polviews, "Conservative", "Moderate", "Liberal")
  )

gss16_advfront %>%
  count(advfront) %>%
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Outcome distribution after data preparation")
```

There are **`r nrow(gss16_advfront)` complete observations**, from
`r nrow(gss16)` original rows. "Not agree" includes "Dont know" as instructed;
it does not mean that every respondent in this group actively disagrees.
These are observational, complete-case analyses without survey weights.
Associations should not be interpreted as causal effects, and the results
cannot automatically be generalised to all US adults.

## Exercise 1: Create a linear regression model

#### Exercise 1 (a)

```{r linear-model-1}
email_mod_1 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ, data = gss16_advfront)
email_coef_1 <- tidy(email_mod_1, conf.int = TRUE)
knitr::kable(email_coef_1, digits = 4,
             caption = "Simple linear regression coefficients")
```

The fitted line is

\[
\widehat{\text{emailhr}} =
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[1]], 3)` +
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[2]], 3)`\,\text{educ}.
\]

Each additional year of education is associated with an estimated
**`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[2]], 3)` additional hours spent on email per week**,
on average. The fitted value estimates mean weekly email hours for a given
education level; `emailhr` is the response, so there is no separate
`emailhr` regression coefficient. The intercept is
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[1]], 3)` hours at zero years of education.
This negative prediction is not physically meaningful and illustrates a
limitation of using a straight line for a non-negative response.

#### Exercise 1 (b)

```{r linear-model-1-fit}
email_glance_1 <- glance(email_mod_1)
# Display all columns returned by glance() in a readable vertical table.
email_glance_1 %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 6, caption = "All model fit statistics from glance()")
```

The model has an R-squared of **`r round(email_glance_1$r.squared, 4)`**,
so education explains only **`r round(100 * email_glance_1$r.squared, 2)`%**
of the observed variation in weekly email hours. The adjusted R-squared is
`r round(email_glance_1$adj.r.squared, 4)`. The residual standard error is
`r round(email_glance_1$sigma, 2)` hours per week, indicating substantial
unexplained variation. The overall F-test gives
F(`r email_glance_1$df`, `r email_glance_1$df.residual`) =
`r round(email_glance_1$statistic, 2)` and
p = `r format(email_glance_1$p.value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`.
Thus there is evidence of an association, but statistical significance does
not imply useful predictive performance.

```{r scatterplot, fig.cap="Weekly email hours versus years of education, with the fitted regression line."}
ggplot(gss16_advfront, aes(x = educ, y = emailhr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "#28536B") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#C05A32", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Years of education", y = "Email hours per week")
```

```{r linear-diagnostics, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Residual diagnostics for the simple linear regression."}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 2))
plot(email_mod_1, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5))
par(old_par)
```

The residual-versus-fitted plot shows a non-uniform vertical spread, with
large positive residuals at higher fitted values. The scale-location plot
also shows increasing residual spread, making constant error variance
questionable. The residual smoother trends down rather than remaining
horizontal around zero, which also raises doubts about the linear mean
relationship. The Q-Q plot departs strongly from the reference line in the
upper tail, indicating right-skewed, non-normal residuals and large outliers.
The residual-versus-leverage plot helps identify observations that could
influence the fitted line. The model also predicts negative hours at very
low education levels.

The plots do not establish that errors are independent; this depends on the
survey design, and respondents may be clustered. Overall, the low R-squared
and problematic residual distribution make this model weak for individual
predictions. Conventional standard errors and hypothesis tests should also
be interpreted cautiously because their assumptions are questionable.
